Whole text (13 pp, 665 extracted text lines) a full-text search for stress/accent: the single hit 'accent' (p.23) is the gloss of a Huron verb ak8a,annen 'to speak a language badly, to have a strange accent' in the etymology of an Algonquian group's name, not a prosodic statement. The Erie content is the ethnonym etymology quoted above (identity quote, not a stress/tone statement), confirming the searcher's expectation 'ethnonym etymologies only'.

sources.note: No stress/tone statement possible: 'Both Neutral and Erie have been extinct a long time, while Erie is completely undocumented.' Eries described as Iroquoian-speaking affiliates of the Neutrals; Huron the likely intertribal medium.

sources.citation: Engelbrecht, William. 1991. 'Erie.' The Bulletin: Journal of the New York State Archaeological Association 102 (Spring 1991): 2-12.
sources.note: No phonology content. Sections: Information on the Erie (historic references, Huron-language ethnonym etymologies after Wright 1974 and Steckley 1985, village names Rigué and Gentaienton from the Jesuit Relations), The Eastern End of Lake Erie, site sequences and ceramic patterning, references. Nothing on Erie speech, sounds, stress, accent or tone; no Erie-language forms exist to describe.

sources.citation: Steckley, John L. 1985. 'A Tale of Two Peoples.' Arch Notes (Newsletter of the Ontario Archaeological Society) 85-4 (July/August 1985): 9-15.
sources.note: No phonology content. Ethnonym etymologies via Huron (Potier), Mohawk, Oneida and Cayuga lexemes (e.g. Huron,arak8a 'sun', Cayuga kahkwa 'sun', Mohawk skaheto'wane 'large field'); argues the two name series denote one people allied to the Andaste. Nothing on stress, accent or tone of any language, and no Erie forms.

sources.citation: Hoffman, Bernard G. 1964. 'Observations on Certain Ancient Tribes of the Northern Appalachian Province.' Anthropological Papers No. 70, Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 191, 191-245. Washington: Smithsonian Institution.
sources.note: No phonology content. The only 'linguistic evidence' is onomastic: 'riquehronnon, the Iroquois name for the Erie of Rique', the stem 'haga/haka' 'people of', and the proposal that Rickohockan = 'People of Rique'. Nothing on Erie sounds, stress or tone.
